claim: Lung cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer which also causes the highest burden of mortality amongst all malignant tumors worldwide.
source: Lung cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer which also causes the highest burden of mortality amongst all malignant tumors worldwide (Siegel et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2021

claim: Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) accounts for 15% of all lung cancers.
source: Based on their histological features, lung tumors are divided into two major groups: (1) small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC), which accounts for 15% of all lung cancers, and (2) non-SCLC (NSCLC), which comprises 85% of all lung cancers (Travis, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Travis, 2012

claim: Non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) comprises 85% of all lung cancers.
source: Based on their histological features, lung tumors are divided into two major groups: (1) small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC), which accounts for 15% of all lung cancers, and (2) non-SCLC (NSCLC), which comprises 85% of all lung cancers (Travis, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Travis, 2012

claim: NSCLCs are subclassified into adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma.
source: NSCLCs are further subclassified into adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma (Travis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Travis et al., 2015

claim: The 5-year survival rate of lung cancer patients decreases from 56% to only about 6% in the presence of metastasis.
source: The fact that a large group of patients has advanced disease stage at time of diagnosis explains the low 5-year survival rate of lung cancer patients, which decreases from 56% to only about 6% in the presence of metastasis (Siegel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2019

claim: Lung cancer survival rate is the lowest compared with other common metastatic cancer types such as prostate, breast, and colorectal cancers.
source: This survival rate is the lowest compared with other common (metastatic) cancer types such as prostate, breast, and colorectal cancers (Bray et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bray et al., 2018

claim: The reduction in lung cancer mortality during the last three decades can be attributed to the reduction of smoking, developments in early diagnosis, and new therapeutic modalities.
source: However, during the last three decades, we have witnessed a significant decline in lung cancer mortality that can be attributed to (i) the reduction of smoking, (ii) the promising developments in early diagnosis and (iii) new therapeutic modalities (Siegel et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2021

claim: Novel screening concepts have proven that the frequency of devastating advanced stage disease can be reduced by earlier diagnosis.
source: Broader public awareness of lung cancer and its relevant clinical signs as well as the initiation of novel screening concepts have proven that the frequency of devastating advanced stage disease can be reduced by earlier diagnosis (Jones and Baldwin, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jones and Baldwin, 2018

claim: Lung cancers belong to the most highly mutated tumors.
source: These insights not only expanded lung tumor classification beyond histology, but also revealed that lung cancers belong to the most highly mutated tumors (Alexandrov et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alexandrov et al., 2013

claim: KRAS, EGFR, ALK, TP53 and LKB1 are the most commonly mutated genes in lung tumors.
source: Specifically, profiling of the mutated genes of lung tumors revealed Kirsten rat sarcoma (KRAS), EGFR, anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), TP53 and liver kinase B1 (LKB1) as the most commonly mutated genes (Skoulidis and Heymach, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Skoulidis and Heymach, 2019

claim: Non-transformed cells in the tumor have pivotal roles in tumor initiation, progression and metastasis.
source: Importantly, the non-transformed cells are not just passive bystanders, but have pivotal roles in tumor initiation, progression and metastasis (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Baghban et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011 and Baghban et al., 2020

claim: The tumor microenvironment is a double-edged sword that has anti-tumor activities early on but may promote tumor progression at later stages.
source: The TME is a double-edged sword that has anti-tumor activities early on but may promote tumor progression at later stages.
evidence: This is a general statement about TME function based on the review's synthesis of evidence

claim: Pro-tumorigenic/immunosuppressive cells include pro-tumor M2-macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and regulatory T (Treg) cells.
source: The cellular TME components can be categorized into (i) pro-tumorigenic / immunosuppressive cells including pro-tumor M2-macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and regulatory T (Treg) cells, and (ii) anti-tumorigenic immune effector cells, such as anti-tumor M1-macrophages, cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells (Duan et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duan et al., 2020 and Zheng et al., 2017

claim: Anti-tumorigenic immune effector cells include anti-tumor M1-macrophages, cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells.
source: The cellular TME components can be categorized into (i) pro-tumorigenic / immunosuppressive cells including pro-tumor M2-macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and regulatory T (Treg) cells, and (ii) anti-tumorigenic immune effector cells, such as anti-tumor M1-macrophages, cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells (Duan et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duan et al., 2020 and Zheng et al., 2017

claim: Immune checkpoint inhibitors disrupt the negative regulation of T cell activity by cancer cells through the interaction of PD-L1 with PD-1.
source: These therapeutic antibodies disrupt the negative regulation of T cell activity by cancer cells which is mediated by the interaction of programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1, upregulated on cancer cells) with programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1, (up)regulated on T cells) within the TME (Iwai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iwai et al., 2017

claim: Only a subgroup of patients respond effectively to immune checkpoint inhibitors.
source: Although ICIs showed promising clinical outcomes in cancer patients, often only a subgroup of patients respond effectively (Robert, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Robert, 2020

claim: Tumor doubling times (around 60–200 days) are orders of magnitude slower than cancer cell doubling times (around 1–2 days).
source: One argument supporting this concept is the observation that tumor doubling times (around 60–200 days) is orders of magnitude slower than cancer cell doubling times (around 1–2 days).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supporting the concept of NME suppressive function

claim: The majority of cancer cells usually die before they can divide and establish a tumor mass.
source: This argues for a suppressive function of the NME and as a result the majority of cancer cells usually die before they can divide and establish a tumor mass (Klein, 2009; Greaves and Maley, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klein, 2009 and Greaves and Maley, 2012

claim: Tumor mutational burden (TMB) is associated with outcomes in patients treated with immunotherapy.
source: One of the key clinical observations in support of the relation between the genomic landscape of lung cancer cells and the TME is the association with tumor mutational burden (TMB), defined as the number of non-synonymous somatic mutations per megabase of tumor DNA, and the outcomes in patients treated with immunotherapy (Litchfield et al., 2021; Snyder et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Litchfield et al., 2021 and Snyder et al., 2014

claim: Recognition of cancer cells by immune cells mainly relies on presentation of tumor-specific antigens by MHC molecules on the surface of cancer cells.
source: Recognition of cancer cells by immune cells mainly relies on presentation of tumor-specific antigens by the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules on the surface of cancer cells which prime and activate the immune cells that can ultimately trigger cancer cell death (Schreiber et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schreiber et al., 2011

claim: TMB can serve as an indicator of neoantigen load of a tumor.
source: Despite the fact that not all somatic mutations will lead to neoantigens, TMB can serves as an indicator of neoantigen load of a tumor (Zou et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zou et al., 2021

claim: Common lung tumor mutations, including KRAS and TP53, are characterized by a high TMB and numerous somatic mutations, which are associated with increased tumor immunogenicity.
source: In addition, common lung tumor mutations, including KRAS and TP53, are characterized by a high TMB and numerous somatic mutations, which are associated with increased tumor immunogenicity (Dong et al., 2017b; Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2017b and Gao et al., 2020

claim: High TMB correlates with a greater probability of harboring neoantigens and cancer cell driver mutations.
source: Thus, high TMB correlates with a greater probability of harboring neoantigens and cancer cell driver mutations (Chan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chan et al., 2019

claim: High TMB boosts tumor immunogenicity because more neoantigens are recognized by cytotoxic T cells, which promote the antitumor immune response.
source: High TMB in turn will boost tumor immunogenicity, because more neoantigens are recognized by cytotoxic T cells, which promote the antitumor immune response (Rizvi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rizvi et al., 2015

claim: In the KEYNOTE-158 study, tumor TMB-high status characterized a subgroup of patients with advanced solid tumors who showed significant tumor remission in response to pembrolizumab.
source: In the KEYNOTE-158 study, tumor TMB-high status characterized a subgroup of patients with advanced solid tumors who showed a significant tumor remission in response to the anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody pembrolizumab (Marabelle et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marabelle et al., 2020

claim: In the CHECKMATE-026 study, high TMB patients treated with nivolumab showed a longer progression-free survival (9.7 vs 5.8 months; HR = 0.62) and higher response rates (47 vs 28%) than patients with the same TMB receiving chemotherapy.
source: High TMB patients treated with the anti PD-1 antibody nivolumab showed a longer progression-free survival (PFS; 9.7 vs 5.8 months; HR  = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.38–1.00) and higher response rates (47 vs 28%) than patients with the same TMB receiving chemotherapy.
evidence: Data from the CHECKMATE-026 study

claim: In the CHECKMATE-026 study, patients with both high TMB and PD-L1 expression in more than 50% of tumor cells had a higher response rate (75%) compared to patients with only one of these factors.
source: Moreover, patients with both high TMB and PD-L1 expression in more than 50% of the tumor cells had a higher response rate (75%) compared to patients with only one of these factors (32% among patients with a high tumor-mutation burden only and 34% among those with a PD-L1 expression level of ≥50% only; Carbone et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carbone et al., 2016

claim: In the CHECKMATE-227 study, combined treatment with nivolumab plus ipilimumab resulted in a longer PFS compared to chemotherapy (7.2 vs 5.5 months; HR = 0.58) in patients with advanced NSCLC and a TMB status of at least 10 mutations per megabase.
source: In the CHECKMATE-227 study, patients with advanced NSCLC and a TMB status of at least 10 mutations per megabase, the combined treatment with nivolumab plus ipilimumab, an antibody targeting the global negative T cell regulator Cytotoxic T lymphocyte-Associated antigen (CTLA-4), resulted in a longer PFS compared to the chemotherapy group (7.2 vs 5.5 months; HR  = 0.58, 97.5% CI: 0.41–0.81, p < 0.001) (Hellmann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hellmann et al., 2018

claim: Aneuploidy is positively correlated with the number of mutations in most types of cancer including lung tumor.
source: Aneuploidy has been shown to be positively correlated with the number of mutations in the most types of cancer including lung tumor (Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2018

claim: Tumor aneuploidy negatively correlates with markers of immune evasion and number of tumor-infiltrating leukocytes.
source: Three groups independently indicated that tumor aneuploidy negatively correlates with markers of immune evasion and number of tumor-infiltrating leukocytes (Davoli et al., 2017; Xian et al., 2021; Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davoli et al., 2017, Xian et al., 2021, and Taylor et al., 2018

claim: Highly aneuploid tumors show significantly reduced expression of genes associated with adaptive immunity, high cytotoxic activity mediated by CD8+ T cells and pathways related to pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Davoli et al. reported a significantly reduced expression of genes associated with adaptive immunity, high cytotoxic activity mediated by CD8+ T cells and pathways related to the presence of pro-inflammatory cytokines in high aneuploid tumors.
evidence: Findings from Davoli et al. study

claim: Highly aneuploid tumors are associated with poorer survival of patients.
source: Moreover, they found highly aneuploid tumors to be associated with poorer survival of patients (Davoli et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davoli et al., 2017

claim: KRAS mutations are the most frequent oncogenic driver mutations in human lung cancer cells.
source: KRAS mutations are the most frequent oncogenic driver mutations in human lung cancer cells (Cancer Genome Atlas Research, 2014; Jordan et al., 2017; Skoulidis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cancer Genome Atlas Research, 2014, Jordan et al., 2017, and Skoulidis et al., 2015

claim: In lung cancer positive for oncogenic KRAS mutations, a pro-tumorigenic, immunosuppressed TME enriched in pro-tumor M2 macrophages, MDSCs, IL-17-producing Th17 cells and CD4+FoxP3+ Treg cells has been found.
source: Specifically, in lung cancer positive for oncogenic KRAS mutations, a pro-tumorigenic, immunosuppressed TME enriched in pro-tumor M2 macrophages, MDSCs, interleukin (IL)–17-producing T helper (Th)17 cells and CD4+FoxP3+ Treg cells has been found (Cullis et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cullis et al., 2018 and depicted in Figure 2A

claim: KRAS is a small GTPase and an activator of MAPK pathways.
source: KRAS is a small GTPase and an activator of MAPK pathways (Joneson et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Joneson et al., 1996

claim: Mutant RAS proteins activate the NF-κB pathway in cancer cells.
source: It has also long been known that mutant RAS proteins activate the nuclear factor of kappa light polypeptide gene enhancer of the B-cells (NF-κB) pathway in cancer cells (Cullis et al., 2018; Finco et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cullis et al., 2018, Finco et al., 1997, and Kim et al., 2002

claim: NF-κB-binding sites are found in the enhancers and promoters of numerous immunoregulatory genes.
source: As NF-κB-binding sites are found in the enhancers and promoters of numerous immunoregulatory genes (Natoli et al., 2005), it is not surprising that NF-κB plays a pivotal role in cancer by fueling a pro-tumorigenic inflammatory environment through the induction of classical NF-κB target genes (Baud and Karin, 2009; DiDonato et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Natoli et al., 2005, Baud and Karin, 2009, and DiDonato et al., 2012

claim: NF-κB target genes comprise cytokines and chemokines including IL6, TNFα, IL-1α/β, CXCL1, 2, 5, and 8, CCL2, and ICAM1 as well as regulatory cell cycle and anti-apoptotic proteins.
source: These genes comprise a plethora of cytokines and chemokines, including IL6, tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα), IL-1α/β, CXCL1, 2, 5, and 8, monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1) / CCL2, and intracellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM1) as well as regulatory cell cycle and anti-apoptotic proteins (Baud and Karin, 2009; Eluard et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baud and Karin, 2009 and Eluard et al., 2020

claim: By secreting IL-6, mutant KRAS cancer cells can activate JAK1 to induce the phosphorylation of STAT3 in immune components such as macrophages of the TME.
source: By secreting IL-6, mutant KRAS cancer cells can activate Janus activated kinase 1 (JAK1) to induce the phosphorylation of the transcription factor signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) which is found in immune components such as macrophages of the TME (reviewed in Chonov et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chonov et al., 2019

claim: Pharmacological blockade of IL-6 suppresses progression of KRAS-mutant positive lung cancer, inhibits STAT3 activation and diminishes the number of pro-tumor M2 macrophages, MDSCs and Treg cells while CD8+ T-cell responses increase.
source: Studies in preclinical mouse models showed that the pharmacological blockade of IL-6 suppresses progression of KRAS-mutant positive lung cancer, inhibits STAT3 activation and more importantly diminishes the number of pro-tumor M2 macrophages, MDSCs and Treg cells while the CD8+ T-cell responses increases (Caetano et al., 2016, Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caetano et al., 2016 and depicted in Figure 2A

claim: Mutant KRASG12V transcriptionally induces CXCL8 through the RAF-MAPK, PI3K and NF-κB signaling pathways.
source: Seminal work by Bar-Sagi et al. showed that mutant KRASG12V transcriptionally induces CXCL8 through the RAF-MAPK, PI3K and NF-κB signaling pathways (Sparmann and Bar-Sagi, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sparmann and Bar-Sagi, 2004

claim: A neutralizing anti-CXCL8 antibody attenuates survival and neo-angiogenesis in a non-cell-autonomous manner and reduces the infiltration of inflammatory immune cells in a mouse xenograft tumor model.
source: Using a mouse xenograft tumor model, a neutralizing anti-CXCL8 antibody was shown to attenuate survival and neo-angiogenesis in a non-cell-autonomous manner and to reduce the infiltration of inflammatory immune cells (Sparmann and Bar-Sagi, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sparmann and Bar-Sagi, 2004

claim: Lung tissues derived from the KrasG12D LA1 lung adenocarcinoma mouse model showed higher concentrations of the CXCL8 functional homologues KC and MIP-2.
source: Likewise, the lung tissues derived from the KrasG12D LA1 lung adenocarcinoma mouse model showed higher concentrations of the CXCL8 functional homologues KC and MIP-2 (Wislez et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wislez et al., 2006

claim: Antibody-based blockade of the CXCR2 receptor reduces the frequency and progression of lung tumors.
source: The reduced frequency and progression of lung tumors following antibody-based blockade of the CXCR2 receptor is further evidence for the role CXCL8 plays in tumorigenesis (Wislez et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wislez et al., 2006

claim: IL-1α or IL-1β can induce the transcriptional and post-transcriptional expression of IL-6, CXCL8 and multiple other chemokines simultaneously through a network of signaling pathways and transcription factors in multiple normal as well as cancer cells.
source: IL-6, CXCL8 and multiple other chemokines (e.g. CXCL1, 2, 3, 5, CCL20, CCL2) are under complex control of 'master cytokines' such as IL-1α or IL-1β, which can induce the transcriptional and post-transcriptional expression of all of these factors simultaneously through a network of signaling pathways and transcription factors (including the NF-κB system) in multiple normal as well as cancer cells from both mice or humans (Gaestel et al., 2009; Jurida et al., 2015; Weber et al., 2010; Wolter et al., 2008; Ziesché et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gaestel et al., 2009, Jurida et al., 2015, Weber et al., 2010, Wolter et al., 2008, and Ziesché et al., 2013

claim: The IL-1 system can be pharmacologically targeted by IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA), the anti IL-1β antibody canakinumab, or a recombinant IL-1 receptor IgG fusion protein called rilonacept.
source: The IL-1 system can be successfully pharmacologically targeted in a range of chronic inflammatory conditions by the (i) IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA), (ii) the fully human anti IL-1β antibody canakinumab, or (iii) a recombinant IL-1 receptor IgG fusion protein called rilonacept (Dinarello et al., 2012; Mantovani et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dinarello et al., 2012 and Mantovani et al., 2019a

claim: IL-1RA is equally effective in suppressing IL-1α and IL-1β, while canakinumab is IL-1β-specific.
source: Of note, the IL-1RA is equally effective in suppressing IL-1α and IL-1β, while canakinumab is IL-1β-specific (Dinarello et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dinarello et al., 2012

claim: Nuclear IL-1α acts as a signal for genotoxic stress and binds to sites of DNA damage and thereby regulates tissue inflammation.
source: They showed that nuclear IL-1α acts as a signal for genotoxic stress and binds to sites of DNA damage and thereby regulates tissue inflammation (Cohen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2015

claim: Lack of IL-1β or excess of IL-1 activity in the lung TME both resulted in reduced T cell activity and a poor prognosis.
source: Using IL-1β or IL-1RA-deficient mice, they found that lack of IL-1β or excess of IL-1 activity (by lack of IL-1RA) in the lung TME both resulted in reduced T cell activity and a poor prognosis.
evidence: Findings from experimental studies with knockout mice

claim: IL-1β-deficient mice showed increased Treg numbers and activities whereas in IL-1RA-deficient mice enhanced accumulation and activity of myeloid-derived suppressor cells were found, both resulting in suppressed antitumor immunity.
source: IL-1β-deficient mice showed increased Treg numbers and activities whereas in IL-1RA-deficient mice enhanced accumulation and activity of myeloid-derived suppressor cells were found, both resulting in suppressed antitumor immunity.
evidence: Findings from experimental studies with knockout mice

claim: In mice lacking IL-17, reduced tumor progression along with improved T cell function was observed.
source: In mice lacking IL-17, the study showed reduced tumor progression along with improved T cell function.
evidence: Findings from experimental studies with knockout mice

claim: KRAS mutations in lung epithelial cells lead to the recruitment of Th17 cells and increased IL-17 production, both of which are associated with lung tumorigenesis.
source: Further studies corroborate the importance of the IL-1/IL-17 axis also for KRAS-driven lung cancer. KRAS mutations in lung epithelial cells lead to the recruitment of Th17 cells and increased IL-17 production, both of which are associated with lung tumorigenesis (Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2014

claim: IL-17 secreted from tumor-infiltrating Th17 lymphocytes can induce the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) gene-regulatory events in lung cancer cells, thereby promoting tumor cell migration, intravasation, and metastasis.
source: IL-17 secreted from tumor-infiltrating Th17 lymphocytes can induce the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) gene-regulatory events in lung cancer cells, thereby promoting tumor cell migration, intravasation, and metastasis (Salazar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Salazar et al., 2020

claim: The blockade of IL-17 in mouse cancer models results in a reduction of lung tumor metastasis.
source: Accordingly and in line with the results from Apte et al., the blockade of IL-17 in mouse cancer models results in a reduction of lung tumor metastasis and the genetic ablation of IL-17C in a KrasG12D lung cancer mouse model improved the response to anti-PD1 treatment (Ritzmann et al., 2019), (Chang et al., 2014; Salazar et al., 2020; Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ritzmann et al., 2019, Chang et al., 2014, and Salazar et al., 2020, and depicted in Figure 2A

claim: The genetic ablation of IL-17C in a KrasG12D lung cancer mouse model improved the response to anti-PD1 treatment.
source: Accordingly and in line with the results from Apte et al., the blockade of IL-17 in mouse cancer models results in a reduction of lung tumor metastasis and the genetic ablation of IL-17C in a KrasG12D lung cancer mouse model improved the response to anti-PD1 treatment (Ritzmann et al., 2019), (Chang et al., 2014; Salazar et al., 2020; Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ritzmann et al., 2019, Chang et al., 2014, and Salazar et al., 2020, and depicted in Figure 2A

claim: The numbers of Th17 lymphocytes in patients with lung cancer negatively correlate with overall survival.
source: Moreover, the numbers of Th17 lymphocytes in patients with lung cancer negatively correlate with overall survival (Salazar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Salazar et al., 2020

claim: IL-1α is mainly immunostimulatory while IL-1β that is secreted into the TME is mainly pro-inflammatory and promotes tumorigenesis, tumor invasiveness, and immunosuppression.
source: Based on their own results and observations from other studies, Apte et al. concluded that IL-1α and IL-1β play opposing roles in the malignant process. While the membrane-associated IL-1α is mainly immunostimulatory, IL-1β that is secreted into the TME is mainly pro-inflammatory and promotes tumorigenesis, tumor invasiveness, and immunosuppression.
evidence: Conclusion from Apte et al. based on their studies

claim: In a murine breast cancer model, IL-1β-deficiency resulted in IL-12 secretion by CD11b+ dendritic cells and supported antitumor immunity by activated CD8+ lymphocytes expressing IFNγ, TNFα, and granzyme B.
source: In a murine breast cancer model, IL-1β-deficiency resulted in IL-12 secretion by CD11b+ dendritic cells (DCs) cells and supported antitumor immunity by activated CD8+ lymphocytes expressing IFNγ, TNFα, and granzyme B.
evidence: Findings from a murine breast cancer model study

claim: Treating mice first with anti-IL-1β antibodies followed by anti-PD-1 antibodies completely abrogated tumor progression.
source: Treating mice first with anti-IL-1β antibodies followed by anti-PD-1 antibodies completely abrogated tumor progression. These data define microenvironmental IL-1β as a master cytokine in tumor progression whose suppression also facilitates successful therapeutic checkpoint inhibition (Kaplanov et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaplanov et al., 2019

claim: In the CANTOS trial, treatment with canakinumab was associated with a dose-dependent reduction in lung cancer incidence (HR = 0.33 for the canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo).
source: Unexpectedly, the prespecified safety analysis of the trial data also revealed that treatment with canakinumab was associated with a dose-dependent reduction in lung cancer incidence (HR = 0.33; 95% CI, 0.18–0.59; p<0.0001 for the canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo) as well as lung cancer mortality (HR = 0.23; 95% CI, 0.10–0.54; p<0.0002 for canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo) (Crossman and Rothman, 2018; Ridker et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crossman and Rothman, 2018 and Ridker et al., 2017b

claim: In the CANTOS trial, treatment with canakinumab was associated with a dose-dependent reduction in lung cancer mortality (HR = 0.23 for canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo).
source: Unexpectedly, the prespecified safety analysis of the trial data also revealed that treatment with canakinumab was associated with a dose-dependent reduction in lung cancer incidence (HR = 0.33; 95% CI, 0.18–0.59; p<0.0001 for the canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo) as well as lung cancer mortality (HR = 0.23; 95% CI, 0.10–0.54; p<0.0002 for canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo) (Crossman and Rothman, 2018; Ridker et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crossman and Rothman, 2018 and Ridker et al., 2017b

claim: COSMIC database ctDNA mutations were detected in 65% (46/71) of the CANTOS patients with lung cancer.
source: Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) database ctDNA mutations were detected in 65% (46/71) of the CANTOS patients with lung cancer but none of the mutations commonly found in lung cancer were enriched (or depleted) following canakinumab treatment.
evidence: Data from CANTOS follow-up study

claim: Median time to lung cancer diagnosis was shorter in CANTOS patients with detectable COSMIC ctDNA mutations at baseline (407 days) versus without (837 days).
source: Further, median time to lung cancer diagnosis was shorter in patients with (n=29, 407 days) versus without (n=38, 837 days) detectable COSMIC ctDNA mutations at baseline (p=0.011).
evidence: Data from CANTOS follow-up study

claim: High baseline levels of CRP and IL-6 trended toward shorter median time to lung cancer diagnosis.
source: High baseline levels of CRP and IL-6 trended toward shorter median time to lung cancer diagnosis, suggesting that IL-1β-inducible CRP and IL-6, similar to ctDNA at baseline, correlate positively with a more rapid progression to lung cancer diagnosis (Wong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2020

claim: EGFR mutations in lung cancer cells can upregulate the intrinsic PD-L1 expression on cancer cells, suppress T cell function and increase levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines within the TME.
source: The clinical outcomes of immune checkpoint therapies have revealed that EGFR mutations in lung cancer cells can not only upregulate the intrinsic PD-L1 expression on cancer cells but also suppress T cell function and increase levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines within the TME, which marks an immune escape phenotype of EGFR-mutant NSCLC (Akbay et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Akbay et al., 2013 and Chen et al., 2015

claim: Patients with EGFR mutations have fewer T cell infiltrations of PD-L1+/CD8+ tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and reduced shrinking properties of the tumor in response to immune cell activation.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that patients with EGFR mutations have fewer T cell infiltrations of PD-L1+/CD8+ tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and reduced shrinking properties of the tumor in response to immune cell activation (Figure 2C, Dong et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dong et al., 2017a and depicted in Figure 2C

claim: Patients with oncogenic EML4-ALK rearrangements showed a significant increase in regulatory T cells compared to the reduced number of cytotoxic T cells in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinomas.
source: In comparison to the reduced number of cytotoxic T cells in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinomas, patients with oncogenic EML4-ALK rearrangements showed a significant increase in regulatory T cells, supporting the concept that different driver oncogenes induce distinct immunosuppressive mechanisms (Budczies et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Budczies et al., 2022

claim: MYC activation is involved in the regulation of cell-cycle progression, apoptosis, cellular senescence, and metabolism.
source: MYC activation is involved in the regulation of cell-cycle progression, apoptosis, cellular senescence, and metabolism (Gabay et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gabay et al., 2014

claim: Co-occurrence of MYC genetic alterations with KRAS mutations considerably accelerates lung tumor development with a reduction of the survival rate in mouse lung tumor models.
source: Co-occurrence of MYC genetic alterations with KRAS mutations considerably accelerates lung tumor development with a reduction of the survival rate in mouse lung tumor models (Kortlever et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kortlever et al., 2017

claim: MYC-induced immunosuppression relies on CCL9 and IL-23.
source: Mechanistically, MYC-induced immunosuppression relies on CCL9 and IL-23.
evidence: Mechanistic finding from studies on MYC

claim: CCL9 regulates the recruitment of CD206+ pro-tumor macrophages and PD-L1-dependent expulsion of T and B cells.
source: CCL9 regulates the recruitment of CD206+ pro-tumor macrophages and PD-L1-dependent expulsion of T and B cells.
evidence: Mechanistic finding about CCL9 function

claim: IL-23 boosts the pro-tumor CCL9 effects through the elimination of adaptive T and B cells and innate immune NK cells.
source: IL-23 boosts the pro-tumor CCL9 effects through the elimination of adaptive T and B cells and innate immune NK cells (Kortlever et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kortlever et al., 2017

claim: Blocking of CCL9 and IL-23 abrogates the lung tumor aggressiveness in KRAS/MYC-altered mice mainly by re-establishing a tumor-suppressive lung microenvironment.
